body:
What is a hydrocarbon?

A hydrocarbon is a compound containing only carbon and hydrogen. Hydrocarbons form a major part of petroleum and natural gas. They are used as fuels and as raw materials for manufacturing plastics, synthetic fibres and other useful chemicals.

Carbon normally forms 4 covalent bonds. A covalent bond is formed when atoms share electrons. Carbon atoms can also bond with one another to produce chains, branched chains and rings. This ability, called catenation, helps explain the large variety of carbon compounds.

A compound that contains carbon is not necessarily a hydrocarbon. For example, ethanol, C2H5OH, contains oxygen and is therefore an alcohol rather than a hydrocarbon.

Saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons

The distinction between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons depends on the bonds between carbon atoms.

ClassCarbon-carbon bondsCommon example
AlkanesOnly single bonds; saturatedEthane, C2H6
AlkenesAt least 1 double bond; unsaturatedEthene, C2H4
AlkynesAt least 1 triple bond; unsaturatedEthyne, C2H2

An alkane is called saturated because its carbon atoms are joined without carbon-carbon double or triple bonds. Alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated because they contain multiple bonds. These multiple bonds allow characteristic reactions, including addition reactions.

Methane, CH4, is the simplest alkane. It has only 1 carbon atom, so it has no carbon-carbon bond. It is nevertheless classified as a saturated hydrocarbon.

Important hydrocarbons and their uses

HydrocarbonFormulaImportant fact or use
MethaneCH4Principal component of natural gas; also present in biogas
EthaneC2H6Component of natural gas; chemical feedstock
PropaneC3H8Important component of LPG
ButaneC4H10Important component of LPG
EtheneC2H4Raw material for polyethene
EthyneC2H2Also called acetylene; used in oxy-acetylene welding
BenzeneC6H6Ring-shaped aromatic hydrocarbon used as an industrial chemical feedstock

Successive members of a homologous series have related structures and chemical properties. In the alkane series, methane, ethane, propane and butane each differ from the preceding member by a CH2 unit. Open-chain alkanes follow the general formula CnH2n+2.

Hydrocarbons as fuels and chemical feedstocks

Many hydrocarbons burn in oxygen and release useful heat. Methane, propane and butane are important gaseous fuels. Petrol and diesel are mixtures containing numerous hydrocarbons rather than single pure substances.

Hydrocarbons also provide starting materials for chemical manufacture. For example, ethene molecules can join to form polyethene, a widely used plastic. Petroleum refineries and associated chemical industries therefore produce both energy-related products and raw materials for manufacturing.

Saturated does not mean non-flammable. Methane, propane and butane are saturated hydrocarbons, yet all 3 are combustible fuels.

Prelims focus

  • Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen.
  • Carbon generally forms 4 covalent bonds and exhibits catenation.
  • Alkanes are saturated; alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated.
  • Methane is CH4; ethene is C2H4; ethyne is C2H2.
  • Ethene is a raw material for polyethene.
  • Trap: Ethanol is a carbon compound but not a hydrocarbon because it contains oxygen.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, ch. 4, Carbon and its Compounds, sections on covalent bonding, saturated and unsaturated compounds, homologous series and chemical properties; textbook content consulted through IIT Kanpur SATHEE on 3 November 2026. NCERT, Science, Class 8, ch. 5, Coal and Petroleum, printed pp. 59–61, 2018–19 edition.]

body:
Why are coal, petroleum and natural gas called fossil fuels?

Fossil fuels form from the remains of organisms that were buried and underwent changes over geological time. They are considered non-renewable because their natural formation takes millions of years, whereas human consumption can exhaust accessible reserves much more quickly.

Coal formed mainly from ancient vegetation buried in swampy environments. Under prolonged pressure and heat, this material became progressively richer in carbon. The slow conversion of buried plant material into coal is called carbonisation.

Petroleum and much natural gas originated mainly from ancient marine organisms and other organic matter buried beneath sediments. Over time, heat and pressure transformed the buried material into hydrocarbons. Petroleum is a complex liquid mixture, while natural gas is a gaseous mixture containing mainly methane.

Do not treat all fossil fuels as the same chemical substance. Coal is a carbon-rich solid, crude petroleum is a liquid mixture of many compounds, and natural gas is a gaseous mixture. Coal itself is not a single hydrocarbon.

Useful substances obtained from coal

Coal is used in thermal power generation and industry. Processing coal also produces several important materials.

  • Coke: A hard, porous substance consisting largely of carbon. It has important uses in iron and steel production.
  • Coal tar: A thick, dark mixture of many organic substances. Chemicals obtained from it have been used in making dyes, medicines, paints and other products.
  • Coal gas: A combustible gas mixture obtained during coal processing and historically used for lighting and as an industrial fuel.

Coal tar and bitumen are not identical. Bitumen, commonly used in modern road surfacing, is obtained from petroleum refining.

How petroleum becomes useful products

Crude petroleum contains hydrocarbons with different boiling ranges. Petroleum refining separates and processes these constituents to obtain usable products. Fractional distillation is a major separation principle: different fractions vaporise and condense at different temperatures.

Petroleum productMain useExam distinction
LPGCooking and heating fuelMainly propane and butane
PetrolFuel for petrol-engine vehiclesLiquid mixture of hydrocarbons
KeroseneFuel and aviation-fuel feedstockDifferent fraction from petrol and diesel
DieselHeavy vehicles and generatorsContains generally heavier hydrocarbons than petrol
Lubricating oilReducing friction in machineryNot primarily used as an engine fuel
Paraffin waxCandles and certain ointment productsWax obtained from petroleum processing
BitumenRoad surfacing and waterproofingPetroleum product, not coal tar

Petroleum and natural gas also provide petrochemicals, which are starting materials for plastics, detergents, synthetic fibres and other chemicals. Thus, their value extends beyond combustion.

Natural gas, LPG, CNG, PNG and LNG

The abbreviations used for gaseous fuels describe different materials or ways of supplying them.

  • Natural gas: A naturally occurring fuel mixture containing mainly methane.
  • CNG: Compressed Natural Gas. Natural gas stored at high pressure, commonly used as a vehicle fuel.
  • PNG: Piped Natural Gas. Natural gas supplied through a pipeline network to homes, businesses or industries.
  • LNG: Liquefied Natural Gas. Methane-rich natural gas cooled sufficiently to become liquid for storage or transport.
  • LPG: Liquefied Petroleum Gas. A fuel consisting mainly of propane and butane, stored as liquid under pressure.

LPG and LNG are not the same fuel. LPG is mainly a mixture of propane and butane; LNG consists mainly of liquefied methane-rich natural gas.

Gujarat connection

Gujarat is one of India's petroleum-producing states. The IndianOil Gujarat Refinery, near Vadodara, was commissioned in 1965. It illustrates how crude petroleum is processed into fuels and other useful products. Vadodara is also identified in school-level material as an early Indian city with piped natural-gas distribution.

Prelims focus

  • Coal forms mainly from ancient vegetation; petroleum and natural gas largely originate from buried organic matter.
  • Carbonisation is the slow conversion of dead vegetation into coal.
  • Coke is largely carbon; coal tar is a mixture of many substances.
  • Petroleum refining separates constituents with different boiling ranges.
  • CNG and PNG are forms of natural-gas supply; LPG is mainly propane and butane.
  • The IndianOil Gujarat Refinery near Vadodara was commissioned in 1965.
  • Trap: Bitumen is a petroleum product; it should not be identified as coal tar.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, ch. 5, Coal and Petroleum, printed pp. 56–62, 2018–19 edition. NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, ch. 3, Mineral and Power Resources, sections on petroleum and natural gas. IndianOil, Gujarat Refinery, official refinery profile, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Coal, Petroleum and Natural Gas: Sources, Products and Uses

body:
What makes a fuel burn?

A fuel is a substance that can release useful energy, usually through combustion. Combustion is a chemical reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen and releases heat. Light may also be produced as a flame or glow.

Ordinary combustion requires 3 conditions: a combustible substance, an adequate supply of oxygen and sufficient heat to reach the substance's ignition temperature. Ignition temperature is the lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire under the relevant conditions.

Removing the fuel, limiting oxygen or sufficiently cooling the material can stop ordinary combustion. This is the basic principle behind controlling fires, although the safe method depends on the material involved.

Complete and incomplete combustion

When a hydrocarbon burns completely in adequate oxygen, its carbon forms carbon dioxide and its hydrogen forms water. For example, complete combustion of methane produces carbon dioxide, water and heat.

When oxygen is insufficient, incomplete combustion can produce carbon monoxide and soot. Carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless and poisonous gas. Soot consists mainly of fine carbon-rich particles.

A clean blue flame commonly indicates more complete combustion than a smoky yellow flame, but flame colour alone is not a complete test of safety or efficiency.

Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide are different substances. Carbon monoxide, CO, is acutely poisonous. Carbon dioxide, CO2, is a greenhouse gas. Both distinctions matter when evaluating fuel use.

What makes a good fuel?

The calorific value of a fuel is the heat released by complete combustion of a unit mass of that fuel. It is commonly expressed in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg).

A useful fuel should provide adequate heat, be reasonably affordable and available, be manageable in storage and transport, and produce as little harmful pollution as practicable. A high calorific value is desirable, but it is not the only consideration. Ease of ignition, storage safety, pollution and cost are also important.

Fossil fuels and renewable alternatives

Coal, petroleum and conventional natural gas are non-renewable fossil fuels. Their combustion releases carbon dioxide. Coal and some petroleum fuels can also release considerable particulate pollution and, depending on their composition and burning conditions, sulphur oxides and nitrogen oxides.

Natural gas generally burns with fewer particulate emissions than coal, but it is not a pollution-free or carbon-free fuel.

Biogas is formed when organic wastes decompose in the absence of oxygen. It contains mainly methane and carbon dioxide. Because its feedstock can be replenished, biogas is treated as a renewable fuel source. Methane is therefore found in both fossil natural gas and renewable biogas.

Ethanol can also be used as a fuel or blended into petrol. It contains oxygen and is an alcohol, not a hydrocarbon. Not all hydrocarbons are fuels, and not all fuels are hydrocarbons; ethanol demonstrates the latter point.

Safety in everyday fuel use

Fuels such as LPG, petrol and alcohol are flammable and must be kept away from unintended ignition sources. Poorly ventilated combustion can increase the danger of carbon monoxide exposure.

Water is not suitable for every fire. It may spread certain burning liquids and can present an electric-shock hazard when electrical equipment remains energised. Fire control must use an appropriate method for the type of fire, preferably by trained personnel. In an emergency, people should move to safety and seek emergency assistance.

Prelims focus

  • Combustion ordinarily requires fuel, oxygen and sufficient heat.
  • Ignition temperature is the minimum temperature needed for a substance to catch fire under the relevant conditions.
  • Calorific value is commonly measured in kJ/kg.
  • Incomplete combustion may produce poisonous carbon monoxide and soot.
  • Biogas contains mainly methane and carbon dioxide.
  • Trap: A fuel with a high calorific value is not automatically the safest or least polluting fuel.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, ch. 6, Combustion and Flame, printed pp. 64–74, 2018–19 edition. NCERT, Science, Class 8, ch. 5, Coal and Petroleum, printed pp. 56–62. NCERT, Science, Class 10, ch. 14, Sources of Energy, sections on conventional fuels and biogas.]
